Irene / Redwood team,

We're starting architecture work for our Private deployment with Redwood and need a clear recommendation on the network topology. Our constraints:

Hi Sanjay — thanks for the clear constraints. High level thoughts below (I'll attach a one-pager with a checklist).

Short summary (TL;DR):
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): fastest to stand up for a POC. Pros: quick, supports existing on-prem NAT/LBs, easy to validate routing and metrics. Cons: typically higher jitter/variable latency, requires NAT/egress IP management, and it's a network-level trust boundary that can be broad unless tightly scoped.
- PrivateLink / private endpoint: best fit for production where you need narrow, service-level access and no public egress. Pros: traffic stays within cloud provider backbone (no public IPs), supports private DNS and access-control at the endpoint level. Cons: requires endpoint provisioning in the customer's VPC and edge-cases for on-prem customers that don't have a cloud VPC (we can offer a partner-managed VPC).
- VPC peering: lowest latency when both sides are in the same cloud account/region and peering is supported. Cons: not feasible across different cloud providers/tenants for many customers; peering also requires route table discipline and can complicate multi-account architectures.
- Application-level proxy (reverse proxy inside your edge VPC): gives fine-grained controls (mTLS, authz) and can implement per-route rate-limiting, but it pushes complexity to your app infra and still needs a secure transport (VPN or private endpoint) underneath.

Suggested pragmatic POC path (we recommend a staged approach):
1) Short POC (Week 1): Stand up a site-to-site VPN between Acme and a sandbox VPC we control to validate latency, failover, and ACLs.
2) Mid-stage (Week 2-3): Provision a PrivateLink endpoint in your VPC (or in a partner-managed VPC if you don't have an eligible cloud account) and test with production-like traffic, validate DNS and IAM restrictions.
3) Production decision: If latency SLOs can't be met with PrivateLink alone, evaluate a peering or co-located tenant arrangement (requires account-level changes).

Operational notes:
- Egress IPs and IP whitelisting: with S2S you need to bake in static egress NAT if your security team requires stable source IPs. PrivateLink avoids that by terminating at an interface endpoint.
- Monitoring: we'll provide per-route token-level latency and per-request traces during the POC so you can map application-level impact.
- Fallback: we recommend implementing an automatic fallback policy in the SDK — if PrivateLink latency spikes, route to a lower-latency regional endpoint with strict logging.

I've attached a short tradeoffs PDF and a mutual action plan spreadsheet to this thread. Connor/Ben/Kim — please add any operational caveats (egress billing, SLA notes).

Action items:

- (Acme) Confirm a sandbox IP range we can peer/route to and any ACL restrictions.

Best,

Adding a couple operational notes inline — quoting Irene below for context:

> - Egress IPs and IP whitelisting: with S2S you need to bake in static egress NAT if your security team requires stable source IPs. PrivateLink avoids that by terminating at an interface endpoint.

Two extra points:
- Billing and cross-account charges: PrivateLink often shows up as interface endpoint charges + data processing fees; we'll provide an estimate for expected egress volume so you can compare to VPN data transfer costs.
- Session resilience: IPsec tunnels are fine for short bursts but if you need predictable 99.99% low-latency, you should consider colocating in the same region and using a peering-like arrangement or reserved dedicated capacity.
